gist: Atwood describes the true Matter as a pure, passive, imageless 'ethereal glass', felt but not conceivable, absent from defiled external nature, and discovered only by Life and the Fire of Intellect through a dissolution of the Vital Spirit. She sums the work as solution, sublimation and fixation, makes the ass the emblem of the self-emptied subject it requires, and ends with the Plotinian union in which the mind, leaving all images, reaches the First Matter and itself.

notes.point: Contraries consubsist in the Divine Original. The 'ethereal glass' is passive to intellect as a mirror to images. Imagining it as a thing or as nothing is false, for it is both; it is felt, not known, as consciousness escaping into its source.
Formless and infinite, nothing in Idea yet in Being all things, it is the source of life; Ideas pass through it like shadows in water.

The Passive Nature must be pure to reflect the Divine Light unmixed. It is the Alchemists' Matter, Plato's Quintessence, Thales' Water, Parmenides' Non-Being, the Kabalists' Abyss, until, returning by its Rational Boundary in the Freed Will to consciousness, it manifests the Supreme Cause.
Adepts of many faiths agree; searching Nature experimentally, they found and used it.

Nature holds no such Matter: the purest is defiled by external Forms. Bound magically, lacking hands, intellect and free will, she cannot loosen the bond of coagulation on her Inner Light, and circulates into herself.
Phenomena are mixture, unlike their Archetypes. Without magical solution and human aid the Spirit cannot leave its forms; Nature rebukes Madathan for seeking the Stone without dissolution.

Casual seekers, trusting an alert mind or a sleepwalker, are warned: only Life and the Fire of Intellect find the True matter, by dissolving the Vital Spirit. Sin's strength is in the Law of dual generation.
Latin verse: dissolve the Stone as the wise do, with no corrosive (our translation).
The art is solution, sublimation and fixation, reiterated with long labours of body and mind. The spirit begins heavy, fantastic and rebellious.

The Sphinx carried on an ass signifies reduction to simple Being without passion, will, imagination or thought; the ass also figures patient suffering until Wisdom appears under the cross of dissolution.
Agrippa praises the ass as patient, simple, clean-hearted and willing, dependent on Hochma; only one turned into an ass can carry the divine mysteries.
These qualities are necessary in the Philosophic Subject. Honoured asses follow, and Apuleius, turned ass before Isis's mysteries. Nothing mixed, selfish or impure attracts Divinity.

As the Aspirant leaves the statues for the Adytum, the mind must leave all images to receive the Unity of Light; afterwards its contents recur exalted. What remains beyond all things is the First Matter.
The soul, running back from non-being, arrives at itself. In union subject and object are one, and a remnant stays.
Plotinus treats union as a true experimental ingress: become established in Intellect and separate from the body.
The ebbing life's primary motion reunites the alienated Generative Virtue to mind.
Logic bounded about reason's inversion and experiment effecting it reach the same Truth. The ancients' contradictions come from subtlety blurred by common speech.

method.veiled: so is this ethereal glass to intellect
method.plain: The subject is wholly passive to intellect, as a mirror is to images: it neither holds them back nor passes away of itself. Ideas pass through it without dividing it.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60 gives the mirror comparison explicitly; that the 'ethereal glass' is the subject (Passive Nature / Matter) is inferred from 'the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind' and 'Such was the Matter' later in ¶60 (see ambiguities).

also.text: imaginations sent into a percussive mirror or reflective vacuum on the understanding
pervade without dividing, like shadows in water, or more exactly as in a dream

method.veiled: may be felt indeed, not known --- but as an escape of consciousness into its primal source without ideal limitation
method.plain: The subject cannot be pictured, whether as a particular thing or as nothing, since it is both. Its reality is met only as felt experience: consciousness passing back into its source with no limiting idea.

also.text: every imagination concerning it will be false

method.veiled: a weak superstantial prolific nature, as it were nothing in the Idea yet in Being all things
method.plain: The subject is not a definite power or act but a fertile, weak nature: empty to thought, yet in being the source from which all life, increase and materiality derive.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60 continues 'whence every form of life, increase, and materiality also are derived'. The referent 'it' is identified with the subject only by inference from 'the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind' and 'Such was the Matter' (see ambiguities).

also.text: formless, variable, incorporeal, infinite

method.veiled: the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind, pure and indeterminate
method.plain: The receiving nature must be free of every image and mixture so that it reflects the Divine Light without distortion and only the Truth appears in life.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60 states the purpose: 'that it may reflect, without self-hindrance or refraction, the Divine Light throughout'.

also.text: that there may be no falsehood or commixture of images, but the Truth only

method.veiled: Such was the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists, the Quintessence of Plato, the Water of Thales, the Non-Being of Parmenides, and that Abyss of the Kabalists
method.plain: The pure Passive Nature is the alchemists' Matter, and the text identifies it with Plato's Quintessence, Thales' Water, Parmenides' Non-Being and the Kabalists' Abyss.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60 asserts the identities in one sentence.

also.text: styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite

method.veiled: until returning by its Rational Boundary in the Freed Will to consciousness, t makes manifest the Life, Wisdom, Plenitude, and Supreme Cause of all
method.plain: The Matter remains 'Nothing' until it returns into consciousness through a freed will; then it reveals Life, Wisdom, Plenitude and the Supreme Cause. This chunk does not explain 'Rational Boundary'.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60 for the sequence; III.2 ¶61 supports the role of free will, since Nature fails for lack of 'a free will to vindicate her final purpose in life'.

method.veiled: having searched into Nature by their proper Reason experimentally, found Her’s; and used it
method.plain: The adepts found the Matter by searching Nature experimentally with their own reason, and then used it.
method.basis: III.2 ¶60. What 'Her’s' refers to is uncertain (see ambiguities).

method.veiled: the purest is defiled with the imagination of Forms externally introduced
method.plain: The pure Matter is never found in the natural world: even the purest natural thing is mixed with forms brought in from outside.
method.basis: III.2 ¶61: 'in the natural world there is no such Matter to be found'.

also.text: all is mixture and an adulterous manifestation

method.veiled: Nature is bound magically, nor is she able of herself to loosen the bond of coagulation
method.plain: Nature cannot release her own Inner Light, which the bond of coagulation shuts up, because she lacks hands, intellect and free will. Left to herself she only repeats her cycle.
method.basis: III.2 ¶61 gives the reasons (no hands, intellect or free will, citing 'the adept', n45) and the consequence.

also.text: she has no hands (45), nor intellect sufficient, nor a free will
generate in monotonous retrogression, always circulating into herself

method.veiled: Without the magical solution and human aid to fortify, the Spirit is not able to forsake her extraneous forms
method.plain: A human operator must dissolve and strengthen the Spirit; otherwise it cannot shed its outer forms, still less know itself anew in the Universal.

also.text: much less can she conceive herself singly in the Universal anew

method.veiled: Ought they not first to be opened and prepared by the most ancient cook of the planets?
method.plain: The subject must first be opened (dissolved) before the Stone can be made. This chunk does not say who or what 'the most ancient cook of the planets' is.
method.basis: III.2 ¶61: the rebuke answers Madathan 'thinking, in his ignorance, to make the Philosopher’s Stone without dissolution'.
method.voice: QUOTED: Nature (to Madathan), endorsed by Atwood

method.veiled: without risking anything, or devoting his life, as philosophers did formerly, to the pursuit
method.plain: The operator must commit his whole life. A casual attempt, an alert mind alone, or the revelations of an entranced sleepwalker will not find the Matter.

also.text: some entranced sleepwalker will reveal the truth to him

method.veiled: no other Fire but that of Intellect, sublimed and fortified in its efficient source
method.plain: The 'Fire' that finds the true Matter is Intellect, together with Life, purified and strengthened at its own source.
method.basis: III.2 ¶62 names the Fire as that of Intellect.

also.text: Life and nothing but Life

method.veiled: a dissolution of the Vital Spirit and alienation of its natural bind
method.plain: The True matter is found by dissolving the life-spirit and freeing it from the tie that naturally binds it.

also.text: Flesh and blood cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, neither doth corruption inherit corruption

method.veiled: Nullo corrosivo adhibito
method.plain: The Stone is to be dissolved in the due manner, as the wise mean it, not sophistically and with no corrosive.
method.basis: III.2 ¶63 (n46). The book gives no translation; this rests on our own rendering, and fits the stress on dissolution in III.2 ¶61–62.

also.text: Et nequaguam sophistico

method.veiled: solution, sublimation, and fixation
method.plain: The whole work has three operations. Solution dissolves and liquefies the enclosed Spirit; sublimation volatilizes and washes it; after calcinations it is reunited in a more permanent form.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64 defines each term.

also.text: after calcinations there is a reunion into a more permanent form of Being

method.veiled: these processes are reiterated many times, and many labours of body and mind have to be undergone
method.plain: The three operations are repeated many times, at long cost of physical and mental effort.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64; Hermes is cited as having suffered and toiled for 'the blessed Lunary of Diana'.

also.text: to obtain the blessed Lunary of Diana, he had suffered much, and toiled incessantly

method.veiled: terrestrial, heavy, fantastic, and proves rebellious everywhere at its Source
method.plain: At first the spirit is earthy, heavy and full of fancies, and resists at its source.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64 describes the spirit 'in the beginning'.

method.veiled: carried within the temple upon the back of an ass
method.plain: The subdued nature must be reduced to a simple state of being by giving up all passion, will, imagination, purpose and reflective thought.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64: 'this is to signify the simple estate of Being to which such a nature is to be reduced by deprivation of all passion, will, imagination, purpose, or reflective thought'.

method.veiled: the conquered elements return under the humiliating cross of dissolution
method.plain: A period of patient suffering follows, bearing the divine mystery; Wisdom is made manifest only once the subdued elements go back through dissolution.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64: the ass also represents 'the patient suffering that has afterwards to be endured'; Wisdom is manifest only after this return.

also.text: bearing and bringing forth the burden of the divine mystery

method.veiled: this asinine condition
method.plain: The ass's virtues (patience, contentment with little, simple understanding, a clean heart without anger, willing labour) must be found in the Philosophic Subject, or it cannot carry out the work.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64: 'All which qualifications are, in their similitude, very applicable and necessary to be found in the Philosophic Subject'.
method.voice: QUOTED: Agrippa, endorsed and applied by Atwood

also.text: There is no creature, concludes the panegyrist, that is so able to receive divinity as an ass
if he had not first of an inquisitive philosopher been turned into an ass

method.veiled: nothing that is defiled by information, or inconstant, or impassive, or selfish, or impure can attract Divinity
method.plain: A subject that is defiled, unstable, unreceptive, selfish or impure cannot draw down the Divine; any mixture is rejected.
method.basis: III.2 ¶64–65 (Callimachus, n48).

also.text: All mixed unguents are hateful to Minerva.
All mixture of her pure and simple oil

method.veiled: leaves behind him all the statues in the temple
method.plain: The mind must give up every image and thought, self-made or impressed from outside, before it can hold the simple Unity of Light within.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66: 'so must the mind be prepared to depart from all images and intellections, whether self-originating or impressed'.

also.text: the order in which Divinity is perceived

method.veiled: there recurs That also which was in the mind prior to the union, exalted and multiplied
method.plain: After the union, images and earlier mental content come back as secondary things, now raised and increased.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66: the statues reappear on return.

also.text: the statues again present themselves as secondary objects to view

method.veiled: that which thus remains to him who passes beyond all things, is That which is prior to all things, and the First Matter
method.plain: The First Matter is what remains to someone who has passed beyond all images and things: what comes before all things.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66 gives the identification directly.

method.veiled: it arrives not at another thing but at itself
method.plain: The soul does not settle in sheer non-being; turning back from it, the soul finds itself.

method.veiled: there are not two things as of subject and object in the consciousness, but the life understanding and the light understood are one
method.plain: While the union lasts there is no split between knower and known.

also.text: at one and the same time illuminates and is illuminated

method.veiled: whoever thus becomes One by mingling with the Efficient, will have a remnant of it with himself
method.plain: Whoever becomes one with the Efficient keeps something of it afterwards.

method.veiled: a true experimental ingress of the understanding essence to its source
method.plain: The union is a real experience of the understanding entering its source, not a vision or a theory.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66: Plotinus 'treats it as no mere spectacle or theoretical figment'.

method.veiled: separate body from the man and its defilements
method.plain: To know the First Light, first become established in Intellect and separate yourself from the body and its impurities. What intelligence then generates, once everything foreign is removed, is 'the original of all'.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66, given as what 'the philosopher' (Plotinus) continues to say.

also.text: should first become established in Intellect, when he will e able through it, as an image, to behold the Archetype

method.veiled: the Generative Virtue, which was alienated, becomes re- united to mind
method.plain: The first movement of the withdrawn ('ebbing') life back from its farthest retreat brings the estranged generative power back into union with mind. This chunk does not define 'Generative Virtue'.
method.basis: III.2 ¶66, final sentence. Whether this is Atwood or Plotinus is unclear (see ambiguities).

also.text: this primary motion of the ebbing life from its ultimate recessure recreates

method.veiled: experimentally proving, it effects that inversion
method.plain: Logic only circles around reason turning back on itself; the experiment actually performs that turning. Both reach the same Truth: logic in light, by inference; the experiment in life, as Absolute Identity.

also.text: the one in light, the other in life, the one by inference, the other in Absolute Identity

quotes.text: contraries are always consubsistent in the Divine Original

equivalences.quote: is That which is prior to all things, and the First Matter

able through it, as an image, to behold the Archetype

quotes.text: the bond of coagulation by which her Inner Light and principle of perfection is everywhere shut up

terms.meaning: Nature's principle of perfection, shut up by the bond of coagulation.

equivalences.quote: her Inner Light and principle of perfection

ambiguities.quote: so is this ethereal glass to intellect
readings: The 'ethereal glass' is the Passive Nature or Matter named later in the paragraph.
It is the Divine Original of the preceding sentence, or something carried over from the previous chunk.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶60 opens with 'Add to this' and uses 'it' without naming a referent until 'the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind' and 'Such was the Matter'; the passive mirror description fits the Passive Nature.

readings: Nature's own Reason, set against 'their proper Reason'.
Nature's Matter, the subject of the sentence.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶60: 'having searched into Nature by their proper Reason experimentally, found Her’s'. 'Her’s' parallels 'their proper Reason', but the sentence concerns 'this matter'.

ambiguities.quote: the most ancient cook of the planets
readings: The agent of the dissolution Madathan neglected, possibly the Fire of Intellect named in III.2 ¶62.
Some other agent the chunk does not identify.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶61 ties it to the need for dissolution; III.2 ¶62 names the Fire of Intellect as what discovers the Matter, but the text never makes the identification.

ambiguities.quote: the strength of sin is in the Law of dual generation
readings: Ordinary natural generation, which mixes forms, as against true generation from the Formal Agent alone; the dissolution must overcome it.
A duality such as subject and object, overcome in the union.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: III.2 ¶61 'Nothing therefore is generated truly' and III.2 ¶62 'natural bind'. Reading 2: III.2 ¶66 'there are not two things as of subject and object'. The chunk defines neither.

ambiguities.quote: even in the seat disposed subjects
readings: Even in the best- or well-disposed subjects.
The text is corrupt here and the meaning uncertain.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶64: the phrase does not parse as printed.

readings: Defiled by forms impressed from outside ('in-formation'), as in 'Forms externally introduced'.
Defiled by acquired knowledge or learning, against the ass's 'simple, indifferent understanding'.

ambiguities.quote: For this primary motion of the ebbing life from its ultimate recessure recreates

translations.original: An tu nunc cochleas vel cancros cum testis devorare niteris? An non prius a vetustissimo planetarum coquo maturari et preparari illos oportet?
translations.translation: Dost thou think, says she, to eat the oysters, crabs, shells and all? Ought they not first to be opened and prepared by the most ancient cook of the planets?

translations.original: Debit modo ergo Lapidem solvas, Et nequaguam sophistico, Sed potius secundum mentem sapientum, Nullo corrosivo adhibito...
translations.translation: Therefore dissolve the Stone in the due manner, and by no means sophistically, but rather according to the mind of the wise, with no corrosive applied...

threads.note: 'Add to this' continues the argument of the preceding chunk; the referent of 'it' / 'this ethereal glass' may lie there.
'as we are abundantly instructed': the dissolution of the Vital Spirit is said to be taught elsewhere; no source given.
'as in the Practice will be demonstrated': the repeated solution, sublimation and fixation and their labours are to be shown later, in the Practice.
Agrippa's praise of the ass is cited from Vanity of the Sciences, 'chapter next in conlusion'.
